messages.subject: Design, implement and promote species monitoring in R course
messages.subject_clean: Design, implement and promote species monitoring in R course
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

We are excited to announce the upcoming online course “Design, implement and promote species monitoring in R,” taking place from 14–16 October 2025.

This course covers the theory and practice of long-term species monitoring protocols, including Census, Capture-Mark-Recapture, distance sampling, site occupancy, and N-mixture models. Through lectures and hands-on R sessions, you will learn to develop monitoring protocols and analyze real-world data.

Who should attend?
Students, researchers, practitioners, and NGO workers interested in building robust, reproducible monitoring workflows. Basic familiarity with R is desirable but not mandatory—annotated scripts will be provided.

Course schedule:
Daily live sessions from 09:00 to 12:30 (Berlin time), with additional self-guided practical exercises.
Course website: https://www.physalia-courses.org/courses-workshops/species-monitoring-in-r/

Best regards,
Carlo Pecoraro

Physalia-courses Director
www.physalia-courses.org <http://www.physalia-courses.org>

messages.subject: MCgof function
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I was hoping to get some advice on using the newly implemented MCgof function for secr models. I understand that the resulting test statistic reflects the similarity between simulated values (from model) vs observed (from capture history). From the function documentation, a value of 0.5 is perfect fit, and approaching zero is very poor fit.

But what if the value is close to 1? And are there any sort of boundaries or generally acceptable values that are considered to suggest the model is a good fit? for example would 0.3 be considered too poor a fit for the model to be reliable? Or is this test simply a point to be noted when using the models?

Any guidance would be much appreciated as I understand this is an emerging area of research.

Thanks in advance,
Brendan

messages.subject_clean: Differences in behavior in both sex.
messages.body_plain:
Hi Murray and forum,

How to deal with models when one of the sexes is disproportionately captured by sampling? (e.g., when females travel off-road routes, where camera traps are usually placed). Is it reasonable to fix pmix with the sex ratio commonly encountered in the specie, ej: fixed= =list(mix=0.6?. Thanks in advance.

messages.subject: Re: Differences in behavior in both sex.
messages.subject_clean: Differences in behavior in both sex.
messages.body_plain:
Another question: We obtain higher density values in models that include sex as a covariate of g0 and sigma, compared to models that do not model sex. What could explain this trend? The data come from several camera trap studies focusing on jaguars, in which females tend to be under-sampled due to their more cautious behaviour, which involves avoiding roads and exposed trails, compared to males. I thought that models without sex overestimate detection overall, consequently underestimating the number of individuals required to explain the detections and producing lower estimates of density. Is this argument reasonable?.
II would be very grateful to read your thoughts on this topic. Thanks..!
